claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is governed by formation of a stable surface oxide layer.
The initial FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy nanoalloy has an FCC structure.
The nanoalloy will be exposed at 800°C for 100 hours in an inert atmosphere while being characterized by in situ X-ray diffraction and TEM.
The exposure will use a heating rate of 10°C/min and a cooling rate of 5°C/min.
A stable oxide layer forms at the nanoalloy surface under the specified exposure conditions.
The stable oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation and degradation.
The oxide layer reduces diffusion of oxygen into the bulk material.
The oxide layer reduces diffusion of other reactive species into the bulk material.
Relative to an untreated nanoalloy, the stable oxide layer will reduce the oxidation rate by 30%.
Relative to an untreated nanoalloy, the stable oxide layer will improve structural stability by 25%.
X-ray diffraction and TEM can be used to quantify the stated improvement in structural stability.
The prediction applies to FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy nanoalloys between 700°C and 900°C.
Oxidation rate and structural stability may depend on composition, processing history, defects, and impurities.
A comparison of nanoalloys with and without a stable oxide layer can distinguish the proposed barrier mechanism.

contradictions.description: The experiment specifies an inert atmosphere but predicts oxide-layer formation and a reduction in oxidation rate without specifying an oxygen source, residual oxygen level, or pre-oxidation treatment.
The intervention only characterizes the sample and does not specify how the oxide layer is created, removed, or otherwise independently varied, despite requiring groups with and without that layer.
The rule pairs 'not significantly improved' with p < 0.05; under the usual significance convention, p < 0.05 indicates a statistically significant difference rather than a nonsignificant result.
